hints: A triangular number has form k(k+1)/2.
Check first whether n itself is triangular; if not, try pairs of triangular numbers summing to n.
Every positive integer is a sum of at most three triangular numbers.
analogy: Test whether the target is one triangular pile, then two; if neither works, three always suffice.
example: 42=21+21, so its minimum count is 2 because 42 is not itself triangular.
algorithm: Generate triangular numbers up to the maximum n. For each test, use an integer-square-root test on 8n+1 to check one term; otherwise two-pointer search the sorted triangular list for a pair summing to n; if no pair exists, answer 3.
correctness: The one-term and two-term searches are exhaustive over their possible triangular values. Gauss's theorem guarantees every positive integer is a sum of three triangular numbers, so returning 3 after both checks is valid and minimal.
complexity: O(sqrt N) time per test for the two-pointer search and O(sqrt N) storage, where N is the largest n.
